opus-5.5.text:
Well, what strikes me most is that it wasn't told how to play well. Nobody handed it a library of grandmaster openings or a list of principles like "control the center" or "don't give up material without compensation." It learned from its own experience, playing against itself, getting a win or a loss at the end, and gradually working out what leads to what. That's the reinforcement learning story in its purest form, and it's the kind of thing I've been arguing for for decades.

And the result is a style that people find genuinely surprising. It will give up a pawn, or even a piece, for long-term positional pressure that a conventional engine would never value, because those engines had human judgments baked into their evaluation functions. AlphaZero didn't inherit our prejudices about what a pawn is worth. It found its own sense of value, and that sense turned out to be deeper in some ways than ours.

So to me it's a lovely illustration of what I've called the bitter lesson. Over and over, we try to build our knowledge into the system, and it helps in the short term, it feels satisfying, but in the long run the methods that win are the general ones that scale with computation: search and learning. AlphaZero is basically just those two things, search and learning, applied with a lot of compute. And it beat systems that embodied decades of carefully engineered human chess knowledge.

Now, I'd add one caution. Chess is a closed world with clear rules and a perfect simulator. The real challenge for AI is the open world, where you don't have the rules handed to you, where you have to learn a model of how the world works from experience and keep learning continually. AlphaZero is inspiring, but it's a step along the way, not the destination.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what impresses me most is that it learned to play. Nobody told it how. It wasn't given opening books or human games or handcrafted evaluation functions. It started from the rules and played against itself, and out of that came a style of chess that the grandmasters found genuinely surprising, even beautiful. Sacrifices that look reckless, pieces left hanging for many moves, and then it all comes together.

That's the part I care about. It's not that it beats people. Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1997, and that was mostly search plus a lot of human chess knowledge baked in. AlphaZero is a different thing. It's a demonstration that learning from experience, with a scalable method, discovers knowledge that we couldn't have put in ourselves. Trial and error, prediction, improving your estimates of value over time. The classic reinforcement learning loop, and it produced play that the best humans in history couldn't match and didn't anticipate.

So when people look at AlphaZero and see a chess program, I see something more like evidence. Evidence for the view that the way to get real competence is not to encode what we know, but to build systems that can find out for themselves. We tend to overestimate the value of our own knowledge and underestimate what a learning process can discover given enough experience and computation. AlphaZero is a very clean example of that lesson, because chess is a domain we've studied for centuries, and it still found things we had missed.

astra-6.text:
What impresses me is that it discovers ways of playing that people didn’t put into it. You give it the rules and a learning process, and through self-play it develops an understanding of which positions are promising and how to reach them.

It’s willing to give up material for an advantage that won’t become apparent until much later. To us, that can look creative, even beautiful. But it emerged from trying to win, rather than from someone programming a notion of beautiful chess.

For me, the exciting thing is the learning process. It can find things that we didn’t know to tell it.
